title: About Me
text:
LinkedIn 



Hi! My name is Comelia Soltanirad and I recently graduated from Case Western Reserve University with a Master’s degree in Epidemiology and Biostatistics, after earning my undergraduate degree in Chemistry from The Ohio State University. My background has given me experience working across science, research, and data. During my graduate studies, I developed skills in data analysis, statistical modeling, and programming, using R, SAS, and Python to work with real-world datasets, build models, and communicate results. I am interested in data analytics and informatics, and I enjoy using data to solve complex problems. I also have experience working with machine learning and AI, and I am interested in opportunities where I can combine my quantitative background with newer technologies. I’m currently exploring opportunities in data analytics, data science, risk analysis, and related fields where I can continue learning and apply my technical and problem-solving skills.
If you’d like to connect, feel free to reach me at comelias1617@gmail.com, or connect with me on LinkedIn.

title: Research
text:
During the summer semester of my Master’s program, I worked on a remote internship with Northwestern University under Dr. Wenna Xi, where I investigated the relationship between substance use and four suicide-related outcomes among U.S. high school students using nationally representative Youth Risk Behavior Survey (YRBS) data from 2017–2023.
I analyzed 11 substance-use variables, including cigarette smoking, vaping, alcohol, marijuana, prescription pain medication misuse, and other drug use. I examined four outcomes: seriously considering suicide, making a suicide plan, attempting suicide, and being injured in a suicide attempt. I used four logistic regression models to evaluate these associations while accounting for age, sex, and race.
Across the four outcomes, prescription pain medication misuse and inhalant use showed consistent associations with higher odds of suicide-related outcomes. For serious injury during a suicide attempt, prescription pain medication misuse was associated with 3.08 times the odds of the outcome, while heroin use was associated with 2.86 times the odds. Marijuana and alcohol use were also associated with higher odds of serious injury. These findings highlight the importance of looking at different types of substance use when studying suicide risk in teens, and allows us to identify where mental health support is needed.






Figure 1. Suicidal Ideation (Considered Suicide). Logistic regression results showing the associations between substance use and seriously considering suicide among U.S. high school students.







Figure 2. Suicide Planning. Logistic regression results showing the associations between substance use and making a suicide plan.









Figure 3. Suicide Attempts. Logistic regression results showing the associations between substance use and attempting suicide.







Figure 4. Injurious Suicide Attempts. Logistic regression results showing the associations between substance use and being injured in a suicide attempt.
